newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka "green" group to contest power law.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka "green" group to contest power law.

text.p: A Sri Lankan "green" group plans to challenge a new government regulation that allows the power sector to bypass environmental regulations, the organisation's chairman said on Thursday.

The Environmental Foundation Limited will go to court over a notification issued by President Chandrika Kumaratunga making environment protection laws unnecessary for power generation, Ravi Algama said.
"We are up in arms about this and its outcome can be disastrous to the environment," Algama told Reuters.
Kumaratunga's notification, issued last week under emergency regulations, nullifies powers vested with existing environmental authorities with regard to electricity generation.
"Hereafter, they can have any amount of power plants contravening any regulation and a court cannot be alerted to it. We find it very disturbing," Algama said.
He said the foundation planned to pursue court action on its own but would enlist other environment groups to take part in a campaign.
Sri Lanka plans several new thermal power plants to reduce dependence on hydroelectricity after a drought last year created a power shortage, crippling business and industry.

The winter northeast monsoon failed again this year, threatening more power outages, but the government has said it has enough thermal capacity to avoid cuts until the southwest monsoon breaks over the island in May.

Sri Lanka says it plans to invest up to $2.0 billion to more than double its electricity generating capacity of 1,385 MW, 85 percent of which is hydropower, over the next 10 years and that it will switch from hydropower to coal.

The government earlier scrapped plans to build a 300 MW coal powered plant near the eastern port of Trincomalee following protests by environmental groups. Plans are now under way to build the plant in the northwest.
